lead: Active suspension uses a force actuator at each corner to push or pull the body, so the body stays flat while the wheels follow the road. A passive suspension has fixed springs and dampers. A semi-active suspension varies damper force. A fully active suspension adds a hydraulic or electric actuator that can both push and pull. Luxury cars and some electric vehicles use it. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: basic spring–mass–damper vibration from a mechanics course, and ESP for yaw and roll control using brakes.

blocks.text: Passive suspension: springs and dampers have fixed rates. The body and wheel move as the road dictates.

Semi-active suspension: the damper is adjustable. A solenoid or motor changes the damping coefficient many times a second. It can only dissipate energy, so its force always opposes the relative velocity across the damper (body minus wheel). It cannot inject energy to hold the body flat over a bump.

Fully active suspension: a hydraulic or electric actuator at each corner supplies force in both directions. It can hold the body flat over a bump while the wheel moves. The actuator adds energy, so it needs a pump or a high-current electric drive.
Sensors: a body accelerometer at each corner measures body motion; a wheel accelerometer measures wheel hop; a ride-height sensor measures the gap between body and wheel.
The corner accelerometer signal is integrated to give body velocity, with a high-pass filter to stop drift, and that velocity feeds the skyhook law.
The skyhook law imagines a damper hung from a fixed sky. The controller measures body velocity and asks the actuator for a force that opposes it.

F is actuator force in newtons (N); c<sub>sky</sub> is skyhook gain in N·s/m; v<sub>body</sub> is body velocity in m/s, positive upward. The minus sign means force opposes body velocity. Magnitude is F = c<sub>sky</sub> × |v<sub>body</sub>|.

For a semi-active damper, the controller applies F only if F × v<sub>rel</sub> < 0, where v<sub>rel</sub> is the relative velocity across the damper (body minus wheel) in m/s. Then it sets the damping c = −F ÷ v<sub>rel</sub>, kept between the damper's minimum and maximum. Otherwise it commands minimum damping, and the body is not held.
The controller computes F and commands damper current or actuator pressure. A larger body velocity asks for a larger force.

Roll control: in a turn the body leans outward. The controller raises force on the outer corners and lowers it on the inner corners. The left–right force difference creates a roll moment that cancels the lean.
Pitch control: braking dips the nose; accelerating lifts it. Front–rear force distribution creates a pitch moment.

Bandwidth: the loop must respond faster than body motion. It must also cover wheel hop at about 10–15 Hz, so actuator and controller bandwidth is usually well above 20 Hz, not just a few times the 1–2 Hz body ride frequency. Power cost is real: a fully active system draws kilowatts, while a semi-active damper draws tens of watts.

examples.question: One corner uses skyhook control with c<sub>sky</sub> = 5000 N·s/m. At one instant the body moves up at v<sub>body</sub> = 0.08 m/s. (a) Find the skyhook force. (b) On a fully active corner, an electromagnetic actuator gives 250 N per ampere; find its current. (c) On a semi-active corner, the damping can be set from c<sub>min</sub> = 500 to c<sub>max</sub> = 4000 N·s/m, with c = 500 + 3500 × I for a valve current I from 0 to 1.0 A. Find the damping and current when the wheel moves down at 0.12 m/s. (d) Repeat (c) when the wheel moves up at 0.18 m/s.
steps: (a) F = −c<sub>sky</sub> × v<sub>body</sub> = −5000 × 0.08 = −400 N: 400 N downward on the body.
(b) Fully active: I = 400 ÷ 250 = 1.6 A, in the direction that pulls the body down.

(c) Relative velocity v<sub>rel</sub> = v<sub>body</sub> − v<sub>wheel</sub> = 0.08 − (−0.12) = +0.20 m/s; the damper is extending. Test: F × v<sub>rel</sub> = −400 × 0.20 = −80, which is negative, so a damper can make this force.
Damping needed: c = −F ÷ v<sub>rel</sub> = 400 ÷ 0.20 = 2000 N·s/m, inside 500 to 4000. Current I = (2000 − 500) ÷ 3500 = 0.429 A.

(d) v<sub>rel</sub> = 0.08 − 0.18 = −0.10 m/s; the damper is being compressed. Test: F × v<sub>rel</sub> = −400 × (−0.10) = +40, which is positive: a damper being compressed pushes the body up, never down, so the skyhook force cannot be made.
Command minimum damping: c = 500 N·s/m, I = 0 A. The damper force is −500 × (−0.10) = +50 N, upward but small, which is the least harm it can do until v<sub>rel</sub> changes sign.
examples.answer: Skyhook force 400 N downward; 1.6 A in the fully active actuator; semi-active 2000 N·s/m at 0.429 A when the wheel moves down, and minimum damping (0 A, +50 N) when the wheel moves up.

traps: Skyhook damps the body, not the wheel; the wheel still follows the road.
Sign slip: F = −c<sub>sky</sub> × v<sub>body</sub>. Reversing the sign adds force in the direction of motion.
Semi-active can only dissipate energy; its force always opposes relative velocity across the damper and cannot hold the body flat over a bump.
Gain units: c<sub>sky</sub> is N·s/m, not N/m (spring rate) or N·s (impulse).
The semi-active test uses v<sub>rel</sub>, not v<sub>body</sub>. The same upward body velocity can be reachable or not, depending on whether the wheel moves down or up at that instant.

quiz.q: Which sensors feed an active suspension?
quiz.a: Body accelerometer, wheel accelerometer, ride-height sensor.

quiz.q: Why does skyhook force oppose body velocity?
quiz.a: To remove body energy and hold the body still; the law is F = −c<sub>sky</sub> × v<sub>body</sub>.

quiz.q: c<sub>sky</sub> = 4000 N·s/m, v<sub>body</sub> = 0.05 m/s, actuator 1000 N/A. Find force and current.

A semi-active corner uses c<sub>sky</sub> = 4000 N·s/m. The body moves up at 0.05 m/s while the wheel moves down at 0.05 m/s. Find the skyhook force, test whether the damper can make it, and find the damping.
What happens if the sign of v<sub>body</sub> is reversed in the skyhook law?
quiz.a: The force adds to body motion instead of removing it; the body motion grows and the loop is unstable.

quiz.q: Compare semi-active and fully active in force direction and power.
quiz.a: A semi-active damper can only make a force that opposes the relative velocity, so it removes energy but never adds it; a fully active actuator pushes or pulls in either direction at any velocity, and draws kilowatts against tens of watts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses skyhook and model predictive control for luxury and electric vehicles. Research looks at energy-recuperative electric actuators that recover power from bumps. Search 'skyhook damping', 'active suspension bandwidth' and 'electromagnetic suspension'.
